claim: Motor learning depends crucially on the cerebellum across a wide range of movement modalities.
source: Across a wide range of movement modalities, motor learning depends crucially on the cerebellum (Gilbert and Thach, 1977; Golla et al., 2008; Herzfeld et al., 2014a; Martin et al., 1996; Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Smith and Shadmehr, 2005; Robinson, 1974), providing a well-defined neural substrate to investigate how the fundamental principles of learning are implemented in a specific neural circuit.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research demonstrating cerebellar involvement in motor learning

claim: Short-term motor learning in pursuit eye movements occurs at or upstream of Purkinje cells in the floccular complex of the cerebellum.
source: In the motor learning paradigm we study, direction learning in smooth pursuit eye movements, neurophysiological data has demonstrated that short-term motor learning, on the order of a single learning trial, occurs at or upstream of Purkinje cells in the floccular complex of the cerebellum (Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2013; Yang and Lisberger, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to neurophysiological studies

claim: Single-trial learning is tightly linked to climbing fiber inputs.
source: Single-trial learning is tightly linked to climbing fiber inputs, in agreement with the predictions of the classical theory of cerebellar learning (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to classical cerebellar learning theory

claim: Purkinje cells are only two synapses away from the motoneurons that drive the adaptive motor response in pursuit eye movements.
source: Crucially, Purkinje cells are only two synapses away from the motoneurons that drive the adaptive motor response we measure, significantly constraining the circuit architecture that implements the transformation from sensory inputs to adapted behavior across short timescales.
evidence: Based on known anatomical connectivity of the pursuit circuit

claim: Longer term pursuit direction learning may be mediated by multiple sites and/or learning mechanisms.
source: However, recent behavioral results have suggested that longer term pursuit direction learning, on the order of hundreds to thousands of trials, may be mediated by multiple sites and/or learning mechanisms (Hall et al., 2018; Yang and Lisberger, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent behavioral studies

claim: The deep cerebellar nucleus is a prime candidate for long-term learning.
source: While plasticity is possible across many synapses in the cerebellar circuit (Carey, 2011; D'Angelo and De Zeeuw, 2009; Hansel et al., 2001; McElvain et al., 2010; Mittmann and Häusser, 2007), a prime candidate for long-term learning is the deep cerebellar nucleus, one synapse downstream of the Purkinje cells.
evidence: Based on anatomical position and cited literature on plasticity sites

claim: Convergent neurophysiological and behavioral evidence across multiple learning paradigms supports the role of the deep cerebellar nucleus for long-term storage of cerebellar-dependent memories.
source: Convergent neurophysiological and behavioral evidence across multiple learning paradigms lends credence to role of the deep cerebellar nucleus for long-term storage of cerebellar-dependent memories (Raymond and Medina, 2018; Kassardjian et al., 2005; Shutoh et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2015; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Popa et al., 2016; Broussard and Kassardjian, 2004; Lisberger, 1994).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to neurophysiological and behavioral studies

claim: Rapid acquisition of learning occurs at the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse, driven by climbing fiber responses, with limited retention.
source: First, rapid acquisition of learning occurs at the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse, driven by climbing fiber responses, with limited retention.
evidence: This is one of the four main principles stated in the results section

claim: Learned responses in Purkinje cells guide the slow acquisition of learning in the deep cerebellar nucleus, which learns slowly but has excellent retention.
source: Second, learned responses in Purkinje cells guide the slow acquisition of learning in the deep cerebellar nucleus, which learns slowly but has excellent retention.
evidence: This is one of the four main principles stated in the results section

claim: The functional properties of the inputs that are subject to learning are different in the cerebellar cortex and deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: Third, the functional properties of the inputs that are subject to learning are different in the cerebellar cortex and deep cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This is one of the four main principles stated in the results section

claim: The extent of learning is limited by negative feedback from the deep nucleus to the inferior olive, reducing the teaching signal that drives learning in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Finally, the extent of learning is limited by negative feedback from the deep nucleus to the inferior olive, reducing the teaching signal that drives learning in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is one of the four main principles stated in the results section

claim: Mossy fibers relay image motion and eye kinematic signals to granule cells in the floccular complex of the cerebellum.
source: Signals related to eye kinematics and image motion are relayed to granule cells in the floccular complex of the cerebellum via mossy fibers (Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978; Miles et al., 1980; Noda, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to neurophysiological studies

claim: Purkinje cells are the sole output cells of the cerebellar cortex.
source: The information is ultimately transmitted to Purkinje cells, the sole output cells of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge of cerebellar structure

claim: Projections from Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex inhibit floccular target neurons (FTNs) in the vestibular nucleus.
source: Projections from Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex, in turn, inhibit floccular target neurons (FTNs) in the vestibular nucleus (Lisberger et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: FTNs are a single synapse from the motoneurons that drive adapted behavior.
source: Crucially, FTNs are a single synapse from the motoneurons that drive adapted behavior (Highstein, 1973; Scudder and Fuchs, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies

claim: Complex spikes cause long-term depression of the parallel fibers that were active in close temporal proximity to the complex spike.
source: Complex spikes, in turn, cause long-term depression of the parallel fibers that were active in close temporal proximity to the complex spike (Hansel et al., 2006; Suvrathan et al., 2016; Ito and Kano, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on synaptic plasticity

claim: Single-trial learning shows a saturating relationship as a function of error magnitude.
source: Quantitative analysis revealed that the learned response did not increase linearly as a function of error magnitude in the learning trial, but rather saturated as error increased (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The sigmoidal model of single-trial learning was superior to an alternative linear model for both monkeys.
source: The sigmoidal model of single-trial learning was superior to an alternative linear model (Akaike's information criterion (AIC) (Akaike, 1974), Monkey RE: -53.3 (sigmoid) versus -14.5 (linear); Monkey YO: -29.2 (sigmoid) versus -20.5 (linear)).
evidence: Based on statistical model comparison using AIC

claim: Both monkeys demonstrated an exponential decay in the magnitude of the learned response across error-clamp trials.
source: Both monkeys demonstrated an exponential decay in the magnitude of the learned response across error-clamp trials (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The retention constant after short-term learning is approximately 0.85.
source: Fitting an exponential model to each monkey's retention data (Figure 3E, black lines) suggested a retention constant of approximately 0.85 (95% confidence intervals based on four experiments per monkey, Monkey RE: 0.80–0.86, Monkey YO: 0.85–0.91).
evidence: Based on exponential fits to retention data

claim: Approximately 15% of the short-term learned response is forgotten on each trial in the absence of error.
source: Therefore, in the absence of any error to drive learning, approximately 15% of the short-term learned response is forgotten on each trial.
evidence: Inferred from the retention constant of 0.85

claim: Average eye speed in the learning direction scaled with the speed of the probe target for both monkeys.
source: We found that average eye speed in the learning direction scaled with the speed of the probe target for both monkeys RE and YO, especially in the interval from 225 to 275 ms after the onset of target motion (Figure 4B, shaded area).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: There was a main effect of eye speed in the pursuit direction in the probe trial on the amount of measured behavioral learning for both monkeys.
source: A RM-ANOVA showed a main effect of eye speed in the pursuit direction in the probe trial on the amount of measured behavioral learning for both monkeys (Monkey RE: F(3, 6)=24.3, p<10−3, Monkey YO: F(3, 15)=13.7, p<0.001).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The effect of eye speed in the pursuit direction on the learned response from 225 to 275 ms was highly linear for both monkeys.
source: For both monkeys, the effect of eye speed in the pursuit direction on the learned response from 225 to 275 ms was highly linear (Figure 4C, Monkey RE: R2 = 0.99, Monkey YO: R2 = 0.97).
evidence: Based on linear regression analysis of experimental data

claim: Target/eye speed in the pursuit direction during the learning trial did not affect the expression of single-trial learning on the subsequent probe trial.
source: In contrast, target/eye speed in the pursuit direction during the learning trial did not affect the expression of single-trial learning on the subsequent probe trial.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4D-E

claim: A RM-ANOVA failed to show a significant effect of pursuit speed in the learning trial on the magnitude of the learned response measured in the probe trials.
source: A RM-ANOVA failed to show a significant effect at 250 ms in the probe trial (Figure 4E, Monkey RE: F(3, 15)=0.56, p=0.65, Monkey YO: F(3, 15)=0.39, p=0.76).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Target/eye speed in the pursuit direction has distinct and very different effects on the acquisition of a motor memory during the learning trial versus on the expression of learning in the probe trial.
source: Thus, we can conclude that target/eye speed in the pursuit direction has distinct and very different effects on the acquisition of a motor memory during the learning trial versus on the expression of learning in the probe trial.
evidence: Inferred from the contrasting results of the two experiments

claim: The single-learning-process model appropriately estimated behavioral observations for error magnitude effects on learning.
source: The single-learning-process model appropriately estimated our behavioral observations for two different stimulus conditions, one that was more-or-less built into the model and one that matches our data as an emergent property of the model. First, the trial-to-trial change in output following a range of imposed error magnitudes closely matched the learned behavior of both animals (Figure 5B), because this relationship was built into the model based on the data in Figure 3C.
evidence: Model predictions compared to experimental data

claim: The model reproduced the linear generalization of learning across probe pursuit speeds.
source: The model reproduces the results of this experiment on both monkeys (Figure 5C), demonstrating strong linear generalization across probe pursuit speeds.
evidence: Model predictions compared to experimental data

claim: After 100 consecutive learning trials, the magnitude of the animal's learned response was always much smaller than the speed of the imposed instruction.
source: Yet, even after 100 consecutive learning trials, the magnitude of the animal's learned response was always much smaller than the speed of the imposed instruction: neither animal ever exhibited full compensation for the imposed instruction (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The learned eye speed in the last 25 trials of the learning epoch was linearly related to instruction magnitude for both monkeys.
source: The learned eye speed in the last 25 trials of the learning epoch was linearly related to instruction magnitude for both monkeys (Monkey RE: R2 = 0.99, t-test on the slope of the regression fit: t(5)=21.9, p<10−4; Monkey YO: R2 = 0.99, t(5)=18.9, p<10−4).
evidence: Based on linear regression analysis of experimental data

claim: After 100 learning trials, a linear model was preferred when compared against the best-fit saturating model.
source: After 100 learning trials, a linear model was preferred when compared against the best-fit saturating model from Equation 1 (AIC, Monkey RE: 7.7 (sigmoid) versus 1.5 (linear); Monkey YO: 0.6 (sigmoid) versus 0.02 (linear), Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on statistical model comparison using AIC

claim: The single-learning-process model produced single exponential trial-courses that learned too quickly and reached asymptote within the first 20 learning trials.
source: The single-learning-process model failed to predict two crucial features of the true trial-course of learning. First, it produced single exponential trial-courses that learned too quickly and reached asymptote within the first 20 learning trials (Figure 7A).
evidence: Model predictions compared to experimental data

claim: The single-learning-process model systematically over-estimated the extent of asymptotic learning for instruction magnitudes between 5 and 20 deg/s and underestimated learning for instruction magnitudes of 30 deg/s.
source: Second, it systematically over-estimated the extent of asymptotic learning for instruction magnitudes between 5 and 20 deg/s (Figure 7B, arrows) and underestimated learning for instruction magnitudes of 30 deg/s.
evidence: Model predictions compared to experimental data

claim: Pursuit learning cannot be mediated solely by the accumulation of single-trial learning with forgetting.
source: We therefore conclude that pursuit learning cannot be mediated solely by the accumulation of single-trial learning with forgetting (Yang and Lisberger, 2010; Hall et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on the failure of the single-learning-process model to fit the data

claim: The measured retention constant after 1000 trials was approximately 0.95.
source: We found significantly better retention after 1000 trials than after 20 trials (Figure 8A): the measured retention constant after 1000 trials was approximately 0.95 (95% confidence intervals, Monkey RE: 0.95–0.97, Monkey YO: 0.94–0.96)).
evidence: Based on exponential fits to retention data

claim: The motor memory gradually transitions from a relatively labile, low-retention learning process early in learning to a second learning process with high retention.
source: These data suggested that the motor memory gradually transitions, at least conceptually, from a relatively labile, low-retention learning process early in learning to a second learning process with high retention (Smith et al., 2006; Herzfeld et al., 2014a).
evidence: Inferred from the change in retention constants across trials, with citations to similar findings

claim: The best-fit cerebellar circuit model agrees well with the data for both monkeys.
source: The best-fit model (two unknowns, η and γ) agrees well with the data for both monkeys (Figure 8E, black curves, Monkey RE: R2 = 0.99; Monkey YO: R2 = 0.97).
evidence: Model predictions compared to experimental data

claim: Both monkeys had similar values for the teaching signal strength and recurrent inhibition parameters.
source: In addition, both monkeys had similar values for both estimated parameters (95% confidence intervals, Monkey RE: η = 5.1×10−4–9.2 × 10−4, γ = 55.9–68.5, Monkey YO: η = 4.5×10−4–9.4 × 10−4, γ = 38.8–65.0).
evidence: Based on model fitting to experimental data

claim: The expression of learning no longer scaled with pursuit speed in the probe trials at the end of a long learning session.
source: However, at the end of the same learning session, the expression of learning no longer scaled with pursuit speed in the probe trials (Figure 9A, right).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 9A

claim: The change in generalization across the session could not be explained by any systematic differences in the eye speed in the pursuit direction during the first versus last 250 trials.
source: The change in generalization across the session could not be explained by any systematic differences in the eye speed in the pursuit direction during the first versus last 250 trials (Figure 9B, continuous versus dashed traces).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 9B

claim: After 2250 trials, the learned response did not depend on the target speed in the probe.
source: By 2250 trials, the learned response did not depend on the target speed in the probe, in agreement with the right graph of Figure 9A.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 10A

claim: A two-way ANOVA confirmed the differential effect of pursuit speed in the learning trials on the generalization properties of the motor memory.
source: A two-way ANOVA confirmed the differential effect of pursuit speed in the learning trials on the generalization properties of the motor memory. We tested for main effects of probe pursuit speed (5, 10, 15 or 20 deg/s), pursuit speed in the learning trials (5 deg/s or 20 deg/s), and their interaction. For both monkeys, we observed a main effect of pursuit speed in the learning trials (RE: F(1, 32)=46.8, p<10−7; YO: F(1, 20)=31.6, p<10−4), no main effect of probe speed (RE: F(3, 32)=1.39, p=0.26; YO: F(3, 20)=0.33; p=0.81), and crucially a significant learning pursuit speed by probe pursuit speed interaction (RE: F(3, 32)=14.2, p<10−5, YO: F(3, 20)=9.0, p<10−3).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The relationship between pursuit speeds of the target in the learning and probe trials significantly affected the shape of generalization across trials.
source: Thus, the relationship between pursuit speeds of the target in the learning and probe trials significantly affected the shape of generalization across trials.
evidence: Inferred from the significant interaction effect in the ANOVA

claim: After 1000 learning trials, the expression of learning generalized approximately linearly as a function of slower pursuit speeds in the probe trial compared to the learning trial, but not for probe speeds faster than used in the learning trial.
source: Here, different experiments used one of either 5, 10 or 20 deg/s as the consistent pursuit speed in the learning trials and probed with pursuit speeds selected randomly from the same three speeds. After 1000 learning trials, the expression of learning generalized approximately linearly as a function of slower pursuit speeds in the probe trial compared to the learning trial, but not for probe speeds faster than used in the learning trial, in agreement with Figure 10A and B.
evidence: Demonstrated by additional experimental data in Monkey RE

claim: The rules for generalization depend not on whether the probe speed is the same or different from the pursuit speed in the instruction trials, but rather on whether it is faster or slower.
source: Thus, the rules for generalization depend not on whether the probe speed is the same or different from the pursuit speed in the instruction trials, but rather on whether it is faster or slower.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of generalization results across different pursuit speeds

claim: In the first 250 trials of a long learning block, both monkeys demonstrated an approximately linear generalization function.
source: In the first 250 trials of a long learning block (blue curve, Figure 11A), both monkeys demonstrated an approximately linear generalization function, paralleling our finding of single-trial generalization in Figure 5.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 11A

claim: As learning progressed through a long block of trials, the shape of the generalization function changed gradually.
source: As learning progressed through a long block of trials (Figure 11A, pink and purple traces), the shape of the generalization function changed gradually.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 11A

claim: After 1000 trials, probe trials with pursuit target speed faster than in the learning trial no longer showed enhancement of the expression of learning.
source: After 1000 trials, probe trials with pursuit target speed faster than in the learning trial (probe speed to pursuit speed ratio >1.0) no longer showed enhancement of the expression of learning (learning expression ratio ~1.0).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 11A

claim: The changing shape of the generalization function indicates either that the properties of a single site of learning change or that learning transfers between sites with different functional properties.
source: That the generalization function changes across 2000 trials indicates either that the properties of a single site of learning change or that learning transfers between sites with different functional properties.
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in generalization

claim: The circuit-level learning system reproduces data on both the trial-course of learning and the trial-course of the generalization of learning to pursuit speed.
source: The circuit-level learning system defined by the schematic in Figure 12A and Equations 2-9 reproduces our data on both the trial-course of learning and the trial-course of the generalization of learning to pursuit speed.
evidence: Model predictions compared to experimental data

claim: The model predicts that adaptive changes in the Purkinje cell responses should diminish over the course of thousands of trials.
source: The model also makes predictions. It suggests that adaptive changes in the Purkinje cell responses should diminish over the course of thousands of trials (Figure 12F,G) as learning transfers to the FTN inputs (Figure 12H,I).
evidence: Prediction from the computational model

claim: Any single-learning-process model that has a static relationship between learning and error and predicts saturating single-trial learning would fail to predict the linear asymptotic learning after 100 repeated learning trials.
source: Any single-learning-process model that (1) has a static relationship between learning and error and (2) predicts saturating single-trial learning in Figure 3 would fail to predict the linear asymptotic learning after 100 repeated learning trials in Figure 6.
evidence: Based on theoretical analysis of model properties

claim: The two-independent process model fails to predict a linear relationship between the asymptotic response after extended learning and instruction magnitude.
source: The two-independent process model in Equation 12 fails to predict a linear relationship between the asymptotic response after extended learning and instruction magnitude.
evidence: Based on theoretical analysis of model properties

claim: The data add to the evidence for a fast-learning process with poor retention based on climbing-fiber mediated plasticity at the parallel to Purkinje cell synapse in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Our data add to the evidence for a fast-learning process with poor retention based on climbing-fiber mediated plasticity at the parallel to Purkinje cell synapse in the cerebellar cortex (Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2014; Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013; Kimpo et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on current data and cited prior research

claim: The tight link between the occurrence of a complex spike and neural learning in Purkinje cell simple-spike responses does not prove that the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse is the mechanism of the fast-learning process.
source: Still, the tight link between the occurrence of a complex spike and neural learning in Purkinje cell simple-spike responses (and behavior) does not prove that the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse is the mechanism of the fast-learning process and we need to remain open to the possibility that the actual site of plasticity may be upstream of the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse.
evidence: Cautionary statement about interpretation of evidence

claim: The non-linear relationship between learning and error magnitude likely reflects the effects of the retinal slip on the probability and/or duration of the complex spikes that occur in Purkinje cells.
source: We suspect that the non-linear relationship reflects the effects of the retinal slip on the probability and/or duration of the complex spikes that occur in Purkinje cells (Mathy et al., 2009; Najafi and Medina, 2013; Yang and Lisberger, 2014).
evidence: Speculation based on cited prior research

claim: The saturating dependence of single-trial adaptation on instruction magnitude parallels findings of single-trial learning in other cerebellar-dependent adaptive behaviors.
source: The saturating dependence of single-trial adaptation in our system on instruction magnitude or stimulus strength parallels findings of single-trial learning in other cerebellar-dependent adaptive behaviors (Fine and Thoroughman, 2006; Herzfeld et al., 2014b; Marko et al., 2012; Hutter and Taylor, 2018).
evidence: Comparison to cited findings in other motor learning paradigms

claim: Evidence that learning transfers from the fast- to the slow-learning site comes from computational and theoretical analysis.
source: Evidence that learning transfers from the fast- to the slow-learning site, rather than proceeding independently in parallel, comes from our computational and theoretical analysis.
evidence: Based on the modeling results

claim: The floccular target neurons in the vestibular nucleus are likely the site of the slow-learning process and long-term storage.
source: Thus, we think that the fast-learning process for pursuit learning occurs in the floccular complex of the cerebellum (Medina and Lisberger, 2008) and that the floccular target neurons in the vestibular nucleus (Lisberger et al., 1994) are likely the site of the slow-learning process and long-term storage.
evidence: Inference based on data and cited prior research

claim: Mechanisms of plasticity are abundant in the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: Mechanisms of plasticity are abundant in the deep cerebellar nuclei and optogenetic modulation of the activity of Purkinje cells can adapt the vestibulo-ocular reflex, presumably through Purkinje-cell induced plasticity in the deep cerebellar nuclei (Jang et al., 2020; Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Recordings from Purkinje cells and deep cerebellar nucleus neurons following long-term vestibulo-ocular gain adaptation lead to the conclusion of neural learning in both sites.
source: Recordings from Purkinje cells and deep cerebellar nucleus neurons following long-term vestibulo-ocular gain adaptation lead to the conclusion of neural learning in both sites (Lisberger, 1994) and are entirely compatible with the suggestion that the learned responses in Purkinje cells instruct learning in the deep cerebellar nucleus (Miles and Lisberger, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Inactivation or lesions of the cerebellar cortex prevents adaptation but does not fully abolish learned responses from previous adaptation.
source: For both eye movements (Pastor, Pastor et al., 1994) and classical conditioning of the eyelid response (Garcia et al., 1999), inactivation or lesions of the cerebellar cortex prevents adaptation but does not fully abolish learned responses from previous adaptation (McCormick and Thompson, 1984; Perrett et al., 1993), suggesting that the residual long-term learning resides outside of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: For learning in the optokinetic response, lesions of the flocculus abolish the learned response completely after short-term learning but only partially after long-term learning.
source: Finally, for learning in the optokinetic response, lesions of the flocculus abolish the learned response completely after short-term learning but only partially after long-term learning (Shutoh et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Different sites of early acquisition versus long-term storage exist for fear memories.
source: For example, different sites of early acquisition versus long-term storage exist for fear memories (Rogan et al., 1997), (Do-Monte et al., 2015), and in bird song (Bottjer et al., 1984; Nordeen and Nordeen, 1993; Warren et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research in other memory systems

claim: The acquisition of a memory in one structure and the long-term storage of this memory in separate structures is clear from amnesic subjects, such as HM.
source: Indeed, the acquisition of a memory in one structure and the long-term storage of this memory in separate structures is clear from amnesic subjects, such as HM (Zola-Morgan and Squire, 1990), as well as from many more modern observations (Tonegawa et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on human memory

claim: In birdsong, learned changes in the pitch of one syllable generalizes differently early versus late in learning.
source: In birdsong, learned changes in the pitch of one syllable generalizes differently early versus late in learning (Warren et al., 2011), suggesting that early learning in LMAN changes signals that are related to the overall song, while the late learning in the motor structure RA operates on signals related to the motor act of producing the syllable.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research in birdsong learning

claim: In the vestibulo-ocular reflex, different generalization for stimulus frequency for gain-up versus gain-down learning suggests different sites of learning based on modification of different vestibular signals.
source: In the vestibulo-ocular reflex, Kimpo et al., 2005 showed different generalization for stimulus frequency for gain-up versus gain-down learning, suggesting different sites of learning based on modification of different vestibular signals.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research in VOR learning

claim: The general rule is that Purkinje cells and their targets in the deep cerebellar nuclei receive identical inputs from mossy fibers.
source: First, the general rule is that Purkinje cells and their targets in the deep cerebellar nuclei receive identical inputs from mossy fibers.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: In the floccular complex, Purkinje cells and their targets in the deep cerebellar nuclei do not receive identical inputs from mossy fibers.
source: In the floccular complex, however, this does not seem to be the case: brainstem areas that send afferent mossy fibers to the ventral paraflocculus region of the floccular complex send only sparse projections to the location of FTNs in the vestibular nucleus (Osanai et al., 1999; Nagao et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies

claim: The general rule in the oculomotor system is the firing rate is linearly related to eye position and velocity.
source: Second, the general rule in the oculomotor system is the firing rate is linearly related to eye position and velocity, and this is true for mossy fibers in the floccular complex (Miles et al., 1980; Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Limited recordings from FTNs during pursuit learning demonstrate a diversity of FTN velocity-dependent responses to a 30 deg/s pursuit stimulus.
source: Limited recordings from FTNs during pursuit learning Joshua et al., 2013 demonstrate a diversity of FTN velocity-dependent responses to a 30 deg/s pursuit stimulus, perhaps consistent with a distribution of preferred speeds across the neural population.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Pursuit learning never reaches an amplitude that completely eliminates the error created by the imposed instruction.
source: We have always been troubled by the fact that pursuit learning, like other forms of motor learning (Krakauer et al., 2000; Tseng et al., 2007; Vaswani et al., 2015), never reaches an amplitude that completely eliminates the error created by the imposed instruction.
evidence: Observation from current data and cited prior research

claim: Even after more than 1000 learning trials, the adapted pursuit eye movements shows residual errors than are in excess of 50% of the imposed instruction.
source: Even after more than 1000 learning trials, the adapted pursuit eye movements shows residual errors than are in excess of 50% of the imposed instruction (Hall et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Motor learning never fully adjusts for the instruction because of active inhibition of the instruction for learning.
source: We suggest that motor learning never fully adjusts for the instruction because of active inhibition of the instruction for learning Kenyon et al., 1998).
evidence: Speculation based on modeling results and cited prior research

claim: Via the known double-inhibitory pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive via the deep cerebellar nucleus, learned depression of Purkinje cell simple-spike firing could reduce the effectiveness of a given movement error.
source: Via the known double-inhibitory pathway from Purkinje cells to the inferior olive via the deep cerebellar nucleus (Houck and Person, 2014; Najac and Raman, 2015; de Zeeuw et al., 1988), learned depression of Purkinje cell simple-spike firing could reduce the effectiveness of a given movement error by attenuating the probability and/or duration of climbing fiber inputs to the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: Speculation based on known anatomy and cited prior research

claim: Previous neurophysiological observations over 100 trials of pursuit learning demonstrate a reduction in the probability of complex spikes.
source: Previous neurophysiological observations over 100 trials of pursuit learning demonstrate a reduction in the probability of complex spikes, hinting at possible inhibition of the olive (Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The data and modeling render unlikely the alternate explanation that incomplete adaptation is the result of a competition between the learning signals and a restoring force due to forgetting.
source: Our data and modeling render unlikely the alternate explanation that incomplete adaptation is the result of a competition between the learning signals and a restoring force due to forgetting (Smith et al., 2006; Albert et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on current data and modeling results, with citations to alternative explanations

claim: During error-clamp trials, the retention parameter after 1000 trials was measured to be close to 1.0, corresponding to almost complete retention.
source: During error-clamp trials, we measured the retention parameter after 1000 trials to be close to 1.0, corresponding to almost complete retention.
evidence: Based on experimental data

claim: Recurrent inhibition of the error inputs to the fast-learning process promotes slow, conservative learning that does not respond hastily to noisy inputs.
source: We imagine that recurrent inhibition of the error inputs to the fast-learning process promotes slow, conservative learning that does not respond hastily to noisy inputs.
evidence: Speculation about the functional role of recurrent inhibition

claim: Two adult macaca mulatta monkeys served as the subjects for all experiments.
source: Two adult macaca mulatta monkeys (12–16 kg, both male) served as the subjects for all experiments.
evidence: Description of experimental subjects

claim: All experimental procedures were performed in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and had been approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Duke University.
source: All experimental procedures were performed in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (1997) and had been approved in advance by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Duke University (Protocol A085-18-04).
evidence: Statement of ethical compliance
